questions.q: What is a process tree built from?
options: Chaining the parent-process field across every process creation event on an endpoint
A list of every file ever opened on the machine
The CPU usage of each running process over time
A manual log an analyst types in by hand
questions.explain: Each process creation event includes a parent process field; chaining those fields together across the endpoint builds the full tree.

questions.q: Why doesn't a parent-child relationship alone indicate malicious activity?
options: Legitimate processes launch other processes constantly, like services.exe launching svchost.exe, so context about which processes are involved matters, not that a relationship exists
Parent-child relationships are only recorded during active attacks
Windows deletes all parent-child data automatically
Only processes with no parent at all can be malicious
questions.explain: A model that alerted on every parent-child pairing would drown analysts in false positives, since routine relationships like services.exe to svchost.exe happen at every boot.

questions.q: Why is winword.exe spawning powershell.exe treated as a near-automatic red flag?
options: Word is a document editor with no legitimate reason to launch a scripting engine, so the lineage pattern itself is what gets flagged
PowerShell's executable file is itself unsigned and untrusted
Word always runs with administrator privileges
Microsoft blocks this pairing at the operating system level
questions.explain: PowerShell is a legitimate, signed Microsoft binary — it's the lineage pattern, not the file's identity, that makes this pairing suspicious.

questions.q: Why does a three-hop chain like winword.exe -> powershell.exe -> certutil.exe carry more weight than a two-hop one?
options: Each additional unexpected hop down a lineage adds confidence that the sequence is a staged attack rather than a one-off coincidence
Three-hop chains always run faster than two-hop chains
certutil.exe cannot be launched by any other process
Longer chains use less memory, which is itself suspicious
questions.explain: A tree's value compounds with depth — each extra unexpected hop makes the overall sequence look more like a deliberate, staged chain of actions.

questions.q: In the invoice attachment example, what specifically triggers the EDR alert?
options: The lineage pattern itself — an Office application spawning a script interpreter — not identification of a specific malware family
The file size of the invoice attachment
The time zone the user's computer is set to
The fact that Outlook was used to open an email at all
questions.explain: The analyst doesn't need to identify the malware family; the lineage pattern of Word launching PowerShell is enough to generate a high-confidence alert on its own.
